parsed.hook: Woodruff Vineyard sits on a 2,000-foot ridge where fractured shale and sandstone force Pinot Noir vines to dig deep, yielding wines with a mineral grip rare in California. Wind Gap’s 2013 and 2014 bottlings prove this site can stand toe-to-toe with Burgundy’s best village-level reds—if you’re willing to pay the Santa Cruz Mountains premium.
parsed.wine_summary: Wind Gap’s Woodruff Vineyard Pinot Noir distills the Santa Cruz Mountains’ paradox: coastal coolness and mountain intensity in a single sip. The vineyard, perched on a steep, east-facing slope near the AVA’s southern edge, catches morning fog that lingers until midday, then bakes under afternoon sun. This diurnal swing—20°F or more—preserves acidity while ripening tannins, a balance that defines the wine’s signature tension. Winemaker Pax Mahle (formerly of Pax Wine Cellars) farms the site organically and picks early, a choice that amplifies the site’s rocky austerity over fruit sweetness. The result isn’t a crowd-pleasing California Pinot but a wine for those who crave the edginess of Gevrey-Chambertin or the volcanic bite of Etna Rosso.
parsed.terroir_expression: Woodruff’s soils—a mix of fractured Santa Cruz mudstone (a type of shale) and sandstone—are so thin and rocky that vines struggle to establish deep roots. This stress concentrates flavors in the grapes, yielding Pinot Noir with a pronounced mineral streak: think crushed granite, wet slate, and a saline finish. The site’s elevation (2,000 feet) and proximity to the Pacific (10 miles) create a climate where cool marine air funnels through mountain gaps, delaying ripening and preserving acidity. The wine’s high-toned red fruit (pomegranate, cranberry) and herbal notes (wild thyme, bay leaf) reflect this slow, even ripening, while its firm tannins and iron-like grip come straight from the soil’s mineral composition.
parsed.vinification_summary: Mahle ferments the wine with 30–50% whole clusters, a technique that adds structural complexity and spice (think cracked pepper and clove) but can also introduce astringency if not handled carefully. The wine ages in neutral French oak barrels (used 3–5 times), a choice that avoids vanilla or toast flavors, letting the vineyard’s voice dominate. Malolactic fermentation occurs in barrel, softening the wine’s natural acidity without erasing it. The result is a Pinot Noir with a lean, savory profile—more about texture and tension than fruit bomb richness. If you’re used to New World Pinots with plush, jammy profiles, this will feel like a wake-up call.

At this price, it competes with top-tier Willamette Valley Pinots (e.g., Domaine Serene ‘Evenstad Reserve’) and Sonoma Coast standouts (e.g., Peay ‘Pomarium’).
